about: Synthetic search eval set for ScreenRecall v2. Every line is made up for this file (no real screen content, no legacy data, not the legacy blind-split queries). A segment is one window (app + title); blocks are lists of on-screen lines in reading order; 'gen' segments are expanded by run_eval.py (deterministic filler). Labels are 'segment_key:n' with n = 0-based line index across the segment's blocks (generated filler is never labelled). Query kinds: exact, partial, paraphrase, xling (cross-lingual zh<->en), typo, unrelated (must return no semantic-only result). Optional tag: unrelated queries are offtopic (default), near (shares words or a domain with the corpus but asks for something it does not contain), short (1-2 words) or number; related 1-2 word queries are tagged short. evalset.assign_splits puts each query in a fixed-seed tune or heldout half (stratified by kind + tag).

How Coffee Is Roasted
Green coffee beans are stable for months, but they taste grassy and sour.
Roasting triggers the Maillard reaction, which creates hundreds of aroma compounds.
At around 196 °C the beans make an audible "first crack" as moisture escapes.
Light roasts keep more of the origin's fruity acidity.
Dark roasts develop bitter, smoky notes and an oily surface.
After roasting, beans release carbon dioxide for several days.
That is why fresh bags often have a one-way valve.
Most specialty cafes rest their beans for a week before brewing espresso.
Grind size matters more than most people think.

segments.title: Lecture 5 - Hypothesis testing.pdf
blocks: Lecture 5: Hypothesis Testing
The null hypothesis states that there is no effect or no difference.
A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null is true.
A small p-value does not tell you how large the effect is.
Type I error: rejecting a true null hypothesis.
Type II error: failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
Statistical power is the probability of detecting a real effect.
Increasing the sample size increases power.

A Century of City Trams
Horse-drawn trams ran on rails long before electric motors were practical.
Electrification in the 1890s let cities extend lines into new suburbs.
Many networks were torn up in the 1950s in favour of buses and cars.
Since the 1980s a number of cities have rebuilt light rail on old corridors.
Low-floor vehicles made boarding easier for prams and wheelchairs.
Signal priority at junctions keeps trams from waiting at red lights.
Critics point to the high cost per kilometre compared with bus lanes.
Supporters reply that rails attract riders who would never take a bus.
Ticket integration with regional trains matters as much as the vehicles.
Overhead wires remain controversial in historic city centres.
Some new lines use batteries to cross short stretches without wires.
Maintenance depots need large plots of land near the network.
Track noise can be reduced with embedded rails and rubber pads.
Ridership usually grows for several years after a line opens.
